analysis.one_liner: Bars homebuilders from forcing buyers to sign binding arbitration agreements to buy a new home
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in June 2001 and referred to the House Financial Services Committee, then to its housing subcommittee, where it sat and never received a vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would stop companies that build new houses from requiring buyers to agree to binding arbitration — signing away their right to go to court — as a condition of buying the home. If arbitration is offered at all, it would have to be a separate document with a clear warning that the buyer is giving up their right to sue, and the buyer would get a say in picking the arbitrator only after a dispute arises. Any agreement that broke these rules would be unenforceable.
analysis.who_benefits: Buyers of newly built homes. They would keep the option of taking construction disputes to court, where rules of evidence and appeal apply, instead of being locked into private arbitration buried in a stack of closing paperwork. Anyone who chose arbitration would at least know what they were giving up and would help choose the arbitrator after a problem actually surfaced.

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits builders from making a mandatory arbitration agreement a condition precedent to a home purchase contract, so a buyer cannot be forced to waive their day in court just to buy the house.

Requires that any arbitration agreement be a separate, standalone document carrying the statement 'By Agreeing to Binding Arbitration You Are Giving Up Your Right To Go To Court', so buyers see the waiver clearly instead of having it buried in the contract.

Bars the contract from naming the arbitrator in advance and guarantees the buyer a role in selecting one after a dispute arises, addressing the problem of a builder-friendly arbitrator being locked in before any conflict exists.
Makes any agreement that violates these rules unenforceable, giving the restrictions teeth.

analysis.who_pays: Homebuilding companies, which would lose a standard tool for steering construction-defect disputes into arbitration, a forum that generally favors repeat players and avoids jury trials that can produce large verdicts. The arbitration industry would lose some volume of pre-packaged agreements bundled into home sale contracts.

drawbacks.text: Arbitration is often faster and cheaper than court for both sides, and builders argue that limiting it raises litigation costs that can get passed into home prices. The bill does not ban arbitration — it requires a separate, clearly labeled agreement — so much of this objection is about friction rather than substance, but the added paperwork and loss of pre-dispute arbitrator selection could make some disputes harder to resolve.
The bill applies only to newly constructed houses, leaving buyers of existing homes with no comparable protection, so it addresses part of the problem rather than all of it.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core change is disclosure and voluntariness, not a ban: a buyer who wants arbitration after seeing a standalone document can still sign one. The main cost falls on builders, who lose the advantage of arbitration terms buried in take-it-or-leave-it contracts. The protection is narrow in scope but the burden it removes — silently waiving the right to sue over construction defects — is real for the people affected.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Financial Services Committee and then to its housing subcommittee, where it sat without a hearing or vote until the Congress ended in January 2003.

narrative.text: Rep. Charles Gonzalez of Texas introduced the American Homebuyers Protection Act on June 5, 2001, joined by Rep. Rodriguez.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services the day it was introduced.
On June 25, 2001, it was referred further to the Subcommittee on Housing and Community Opportunity.
No further action was taken, and the bill never received a floor vote in either chamber before the 107th Congress ended.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Homebuilders keep the standard practice of requiring buyers to sign arbitration agreements as part of the purchase contract, preserving a favorable forum for construction-defect disputes. New home buyers remain the party left unprotected.

for.name: Charles A. Gonzalez
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and coordinated its introduction with Rep. Rodriguez.

for.name: Ciro Rodriguez
for.what_they_did: Joined the bill as an original cosponsor at introduction.

for.name: 4 of 208 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no Republican signed on.

against.name: House Financial Services Committee
against.role: Committee of referral; chaired by Rep. Michael Oxley (R-OH)
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to its Subcommittee on Housing and Community Opportunity, where it remained without a hearing, markup, or vote for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken; the sponsor and all four cosponsors were Democrats, and the bill died in a committee controlled by the Republican majority without any recorded opposition.

industries.note: Builders would lose the ability to make binding arbitration a condition of buying a new home and to bundle it into the purchase contract, steering defect disputes into a private forum that generally favors repeat players over one-time buyers. The bill died, so the practice continued unchanged.

The bill would have ended the flow of pre-packaged arbitration agreements bundled into new home contracts and required buyers to help select the arbitrator after a dispute arises, cutting into a reliable volume of cases. Arbitration would still have been available to buyers who signed a separate agreement.
